newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan exchange seen challenging CME, SIMEX futures.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan exchange seen challenging CME, SIMEX futures.

text.p: Plans by Singapore and Chicago to offer Taiwan stock index futures in January may make quick markets, but analysts say the island's own futures exchange would be ready to fight back when it opens in July.

The Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), eyeing a gap opened by Taiwan's financial liberalisation but not yet filled by a long-awaited futures exchange, said on Wednesday it would launch futures and options linked to Taiwan's stock market performance.

The SIMEX contracts resemble those planned by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), which have won U.S. regulatory approval. Both will launch in early January with trading during Taiwan stock trading hours, but analysts predict Taiwan's own futures exchange, once it opens, will have strong advantages with which to woo business back.
"The physical cash market is here and a local market is free from foreign exchange risk," Steve Wang, president of Taipei's Grand Cathay Futures, told Reuters on Wednesday.

Wang said small Taiwan investors were likely to dominate the local market's index futures trading volume and, as a result, contracts linked to the Taiwan Stock Exchange's main Taiwan All Share Index (TAIEX) had the best chance of popular acceptance.

Wang said the overseas futures, by contrast, would be linked to lesser-known indices that do not correlate identically to the TAIEX. The CME's contracts will be derived from a Taiwan share index compiled by Dow Jones, while SIMEX futures will be linked to Morgan Stanley Capital International's (MSCI) Taiwan index.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange is not expected to authorise the CME or SIMEX to use the TAIEX, while the planned futures exchange, an affiliate of the stock exchange, will use it.

Several Taiwan futures brokers agreed, saying they expected the CME and SIMEX contracts to sell well initially due to strong demand from Taiwan and other Asian investors, but that they would face a serious challenge once the Taiwan futures exchange opens.
Analysts estimate Taiwan stock index futures could generate T$50 billion (US$1.8 billion) a month in turnover in the first year.
Wang cautioned that Taiwan would have to move quickly to avoid allowing the CME or SIMEX contracts to establish a beach-head.
Eager to keep business at home, Taiwan is scrambling to open its exchange and launch products by July 1. But it still faces a key obstacle -- the lack of a futures exchange law.

A committee of the Legislative Yuan (parliament) has passed a draft law but the full parliament has yet to adopt final legislation. With the year-end recess just days away, analysts said the chances for the bill's imminent passage were fading.
Fearing that the futures exchange could be stalled, the Taiwan Stock Exchange is studying the software and hardware required to trade index options.
Options would not require a futures exchange law, but the securities exchange law would need to be redefined to include index options under the legal definition of securities.
The local financial community has called for the government to allow stock index options in March, and sources said such options would be based on the TAIEX.
Legislator Lin Chung-chan, who has questioned options trade, said trading stock options on the stock exchange could create major risks if the clearing system was inadequate.
"Having no good clearance system in place is like a major financial scandal and crisis waiting to happen," Lin said.
